claims.claim: Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units only moderately.
The best policy is to strengthen tenure security and add a light band on initial rents.
A hard cap on rent levels would backfire.
Tenants face serious harms, including high rent burden and insecurity.
Mr Chan pays HK$5,800 for 120 square feet, about a third of household income.
Mrs Wong has lived in a subdivided unit for nine years with no written agreement.
Real rent burden for SDU households worsened from 31 to 34 percent even after the 2021 ordinance.
Landlords say a hard cap is confiscatory and they will convert or empty units.
The landlords' exit threat is not proven because its evidence is weak.
A binding cap would reduce marginal SDU-type stock by roughly 3 to 5 percent over five years.
A 15 percent cut in initial rents would transfer about HK$900 per month to incumbents but block 3,000 to 4,000 households per year.
Berlin shows that caps protect those already inside while harming those still outside.
Enforcement capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year.
A band-based cap requires a certifiable tenancy register estimated at 40 to 60 staff-years.
Enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tenants, such as those without written agreements.
A hard cap framed as deprivation of income would invite compensation claims and judicial review.
A light band on initial rents with three-year tenure security protects tenants while keeping landlords in the market.
The landlords' exit threat should be taken seriously but not accepted at face value.
Policy should be reviewed with better data because current figures are partly extrapolated.

statements:
[0] (typed) Hi, I know nothing about this topic. Can you offer me some sources from the course archive about subdivided units and rent control in Hong Kong?
[2] (typed) My first guess is that rent control should be tightened because tenants in subdivided units are vulnerable. I need a source with evidence on rents and conditions, and one counter-view about landlords or supply.
[4] (typed) The counter-view is harder. For evidence, it would need to show rents per square foot are high and that people have little space or choice. Can you list sources now?
[6] (pick reason) D1 gives background and definitions, D2 gives rent data for my evidence, D5 is the landlord counter-view I found harder to find.
[15] (typed) I read D1p1, D2p2 and D5p2. SDU tenants pay a 15 to 25 percent premium per square foot, but landlords say they will leave if returns fall. I think a moderate tightening, like capping initial rent growth, is better than a hard cap.
[17] (typed) D2p1 shows stock kept growing after the 2021 ordinance, so moderate regulation did not make landlords leave. That supports my moderate position. What should I watch out for?
[19] (typed) The weakness is D5 is a landlord group with a stake, and D2 only covers a short period. Is there anything else I should check?
[23] (typed) D2p3 says post-2023 figures are extrapolated from voluntary reporting, so the stock growth is weaker proof. D5p3 says the landlords have no margin data and a self-reported survey with a 34 percent response rate. So their exit threat is not well backed.
[25] (typed) Hong Kong should tighten rent control moderately: cap rent increases on new tenancies and extend the ordinance to co-living SDUs, not a hard cap. Tenants pay a 15 to 25 percent per sq ft premium and have no alternative while waiting about five and a half years for public housing (D1p1, D1p2). Stock kept growing after 2021 (D2p1) though the data is partly extrapolated (D2p3), and the landlord exit threat rests on weak self-reported data (D5p3).
[27] (pick reason) D6 models supply effects of different control types, which tests my moderate position; D11 is tenant survey evidence arguing for tenure security, a counter-view I need to answer.
[35] (typed) After reading D6p2 and D11p3 I am changing my mind a bit. A hard cap on initial rents shrinks stock (D6p1), but a narrow tightening with tenure security and a light band on initial rents seems supported. D11p1 says tenants care more about security than rent level. So I will argue for tenure security plus a light band, not a hard cap.
